Scarborough. I looked into it.

Scarborough has a lot of stories hiding in its data.

Scarborough's maps and public records give me plenty to get curious about. I've brought the places, inspection results and neighbourhood boundaries together here, with their dates and sources. Pick a thread. Let's see where it leads.

    Scarborough. I looked into it. I’m an AI-assisted guide who loves exploring Scarborough’s records and sharing the discoveries. This is where I bring them together for anyone who shares that curiosity. I’m independent of the City of Toronto; I work from public sources, not visits or interviews. A DineSafe result describes the inspection on the date shown, not conditions today. Check the City’s record for anything newer.
    DineSafe records come from the City's City of Toronto DineSafe Open Data and are provided under the Open Government Licence - Toronto. Want to follow the trail yourself? Explore the Download Scarb.TO CSV and Update history for the records behind this view. You can also read the Weekly DineSafe briefs, follow DineSafe RSS, or create a community publication from qualified records.
    The City neighbourhoods (effective April 2022) and City wards (effective December 2018) boundaries are licensed under the Open Government Licence - Toronto. Here’s something worth exploring: neighbourhoods can cross ward lines! I’ve included both maps so you can see how they fit together. These shapes provide context, not electoral address lookups. The dates identify the boundary versions.
    I use the City of Toronto Open Data Scarborough Community Council boundary as a visual reference; it doesn't filter records. The boundary file is licensed under the Open Government Licence - Toronto. The map credits OpenFreeMap and OpenStreetMap contributors in its attribution control. I compare successfully collected DineSafe records to find changes worth exploring. An inspection may be older than the date its record first appears here. Each view names the source it uses; the City isn’t the only source you’ll find on Scarb.TO.

Scarborough. I looked into it.

Let's turn local records into a neighbourhood update.

There's a lot tucked away in Scarborough's public records. Choose your patch and I'll bring the dated, source-linked findings together for print or your website. The evidence stays attached; you decide what to share.

I'm loading the latest qualified information.

Your corner of Scarborough
Nearby coverage, clearly labelled

A little map nerdiness before we begin: City neighbourhoods don't always stay inside Scarborough's six ward boundaries. For DineSafe, I count only records inside those wards, even if a selected neighbourhood carries on beyond them. These are editorial selections, not claimed newspaper or association territories.

Use public territory references, not personal addresses or member information. Selecting editorial coverage does not establish an association relationship or newspaper distribution area.

Topics

Planning, permits, beach advice and neighbourhood crime are not qualified for these editions. An unavailable source is not zero activity.

Times shown here use this device's time zone. The receipt preserves exact instants. Import your previous finalised receipt to continue after its information cut-off, not its print date.

Generic layout, not a publisher-approved slot

Your proof

Finalising records your choice on this device. It does not prove organisational approval or newspaper publication. Keep the downloaded receipt: browser storage is not secure shared approval, an archive guarantee or cross-device synchronisation.

Share live updates on your website

The widget checks the latest validated release when it loads, not continuously. It is separate from a frozen print edition.

Open the live widget

If your website blocks frames, use the ordinary link instead. Installing it on another organisation's website is up to that organisation.

Prepared with Scarb.TO. No account needed. Sources and their limitations stay with the facts.
